passage:
I'm Aparna and I'm nine. Last Sunday I lost my chess match to Akash in the second round of the school tournament. He took my queen in ten moves and I didn't even see it coming.
In the car I was waiting for Amma to ask 'Did you win?' She didn't. She asked, 'What did you learn today?'
I said I learned to look at his bishop before I move my queen.
Then she asked, 'What part was fun?' I said the first round, when I did the fork with my knight.
Only after that she asked the score. I said I lost, and she just said, 'Okay. I lose things at work too. We'll practise that bishop trap.'
I thought she would be upset. She wasn't. So I wasn't so upset either. We practised it on Monday.

qa.q: Who beat Aparna in the second round?
qa.a: Akash beat Aparna in the second round.

qa.q: What was Aparna expecting in the car, and how did Aparna feel afterwards?
qa.a: Aparna expected Amma to ask about winning and to be upset, and felt calmer after seeing that Amma wasn't 🙂

qa.q: What worked about the order of Amma's questions?
qa.a: Asking about learning and fun before the score helped Aparna think about what went well and what to fix, not just the loss.

qa.q: How might Amma see losing, based on what she said?
qa.a: Amma sees losing as ordinary and fixable, something that happens at work too, and shows that by planning practice.

grounding: It shows a parent asking a child about what they learned and enjoyed before the score, so the child treats failure as ordinary and workable.

passage:
Note for Mummy, who missed the match, from Sahil (Papa).
Dolma's team lost 0-3 today. She was in goal and walked off with her head down and her gloves stuffed in her pocket, and I could see her bracing for me.
I didn't mention the score. Walking to the scooter, I asked, 'What did you learn out there?' She thought and said, 'When they come from the side, I should move early.'
Then I asked what she enjoyed. That got a real smile: 'The save in the first half! The dive!'
Only then did I ask how it ended. 'We lost,' she said, flatly, not crying. I said I'd lost a work pitch on Tuesday and would try something new. She nodded like that was normal.
At home she asked to practise side dives in the courtyard.

qa.q: What position did Dolma play in the match?
qa.a: Dolma was in goal.

qa.q: What might Dolma have been worried about as she walked off the pitch?
qa.a: She seemed worried that her Papa would be disappointed, since she walked off with her head down and her gloves stuffed in her pocket.

qa.q: What does Sahil's approach show a parent can do after a child loses?
qa.a: Ask what the child learned and enjoyed before the score, and share one's own setback, so losing feels normal and workable.

qa.q: If Mummy reads this note, what might she understand about Dolma?
qa.a: Mummy might see that Dolma handled the loss calmly and even wants to practise, because the questions made it feel ordinary.

grounding: It shows a parent asking about learning and enjoyment before the score and treating his own setback as ordinary, helping the child face failure.

passage:
Dear diary,
Today I lost my first chess game at the district tournament, to a boy called Harsha. I was sure Appa would ask "What was the score?" like everyone does. But in the auto he asked, "What was the most fun move you made?"
I told him about my knight fork in the middle. He said, "Show me tonight." Then he asked what I would try differently. I said I brought my queen out too early again.
Only after that did he ask about the result. I said I lost. He just nodded and said, "Okay. Next time the queen stays home a bit longer." He wasn't upset at all.
At dinner Appa told Amma about my fork, not my loss. I felt lighter.
Swati

qa.q: What was the first question Appa asked in the auto?
qa.a: What was the most fun move you made?

qa.q: How did Swati feel at dinner when Appa talked about the fork?
qa.a: Swati felt lighter and relieved, because the loss was treated as ordinary rather than a disaster.

qa.q: What did Appa do well after the match?
qa.a: He asked about fun and lessons before the score, then turned the loss into one simple thing to try next time.

qa.q: How does Appa seem to see the loss?
qa.a: As an ordinary part of learning chess, something to study and fix, not something to be upset about.

grounding: A parent asks a child about enjoyment and lessons before the result, showing that losing is ordinary and workable.

passage:
The girls' kabaddi team from Aadhya's village lost the block-level match by six points, and Aadhya had been caught on her last raid. On the bicycle ride home along the canal she sat on the carrier behind her father, Uday, waiting for the question every uncle had already asked: "By how much?"
Uday pedalled for a while. Then he said, "Tell me the best moment."
"The first raid. I touched two and got back."
"I saw. What did you learn from the last one?"
She thought. "I went too deep. I should have come back after one touch."
"Good. Anything else?"
"Their stopper was really strong."
Only at the village well did he ask, "And the score?" She told him. He shrugged. "Next month there's another match."
She swung her legs, humming.

qa.q: Where did Aadhya sit on the ride home?
qa.a: On the carrier behind her father, Uday.

qa.q: What was Aadhya expecting when she sat behind Uday?
qa.a: She was dreading the usual question about the score and felt tense about the lost match.

qa.q: Why did Uday wait until the well to ask the score?
qa.a: Asking first about the best moment and the lesson let Aadhya think about her play, so the score became just one fact.

qa.q: What does Uday's shrug show about how he sees losing?
qa.a: Uday sees a loss as ordinary and workable, one match before the next, not a failure to worry about.

grounding: A father asks his daughter what she enjoyed and learned before the score, showing that losing is ordinary and workable.

passage:
In the car park of the community pool in Vancouver, Soo-ah climbed into the back seat with wet hair and a face ready for bad news. She had come fifth out of six in the 50-metre freestyle.
Her father, Chen, started the engine but didn't pull out. "What was the best part?"
"The dive. I didn't belly-flop this time."
"I saw. Clean. What would you change?"
"I breathed every two strokes. Coach said every three. I got tired."
"Want to practise that on Saturday?"
"Okay." She paused. "Aren't you going to ask where I came?"
"Where did you come?"
"Fifth."
"Fifth," he repeated, as if it were the weather. "Dumplings or noodles?"
Soo-ah laughed for the first time since the race.

qa.q: How did Soo-ah finish in the 50-metre freestyle?
qa.a: Fifth out of six.

qa.q: What does Soo-ah's face show when she climbs into the car?
qa.a: She was nervous and braced for disappointment about coming fifth.

qa.q: Which choice by Chen helped most, and why?
qa.a: Asking about the best part and one change before the result, so Soo-ah could look at her swim calmly instead of only the placing.

qa.q: What would change if Chen had asked the placing first?
qa.a: Soo-ah might have felt judged and shut down, missing the chance to notice her clean dive and breathing plan.

grounding: A father asks his daughter what went well and what she would change before the result, treating the loss as ordinary.

passage: At the district badminton hall, Anjali came off court after losing 21-9, 21-12, her racket dragging on the floor. The other parents were already talking scores. Vinita handed her the water bottle and waited until she had drunk. "What was the best rally for you?" Anjali thought. "The long one in the second game. I did the drop shot, like Coach showed us." "I saw that. What did you learn from her?" "She always hits to my backhand." Vinita nodded. "Useful. Want to practise backhands on Saturday?" Only then did Anjali mumble, "I lost badly, Mumma." "You did," Vinita said easily. "Losing happens to everyone. I failed my driving test twice." Anjali giggled. "Twice?" "Twice. Come, let's get a samosa."

qa.q: Which rally did Anjali say was her best?
qa.a: The long one in the second game, with the drop shot.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel coming off the court?
qa.a: She was disappointed and deflated, her racket dragging on the floor.

qa.q: Why does Vinita ask about the best rally before the score?
qa.a: It shows that losing is ordinary and workable, turning the match into things learned and enjoyed rather than a verdict.

qa.q: What is it like for Vinita to hear "I lost badly, Mumma"?
qa.a: Vinita stays calm and light, treating the loss as normal and even sharing her own failed driving tests to make Anjali laugh.

grounding: Shows a parent asking a child what she enjoyed and learned before mentioning the score, treating a loss as ordinary and workable.
